title: Redwood Discovery: Reliability & Incident Tolerance with Citadela Systems
summary: Discovery focused on incident tolerance and fallback strategies across Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Customer highlighted multi-region failover, per-route SLAs, and auditability as key constraints. Redwood AE/SE discussed routing policies, model variant fallbacks, circuit breakers, and suggested a staged POC with synthetic failover tests.
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-04-12
- Time: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~42 minutes
- Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Lina Gomez (Redwood SE), Maya Rios (CTO, Citadela), Samir Patel (SRE), Jordan Lee (Product)

[00:00] Ethan: hey everyone, thanks for carving time, i'm ethan from redwood, with lina our solutions engineer. quick round robin?
[00:10] Maya: maya here, CTO at citadela, focusing on reliability of our customer support ai which is hitting p99 spikes, thanks for joining.
[00:18] Samir: samir, sre, i'll own the ops side and failover design.
[00:22] Jordan: jordan, product, i'm tracking slas and business impact.
[00:30] Ethan: great, the goal today is to understand your reliability and incident tolerance needs — multi-region failover, fallback policies if models or regions fail, and where hosted vs dedicated vs private fit. does that match expectations?
[00:42] Maya: yes, we run a chat assistant integrated into our web and mobile. we need <200ms p50, and p99 ideally under 700ms but we accept higher if fallback ensures availability. main ask: when incidents happen we cannot drop requests silently; need clear fallbacks and an SLA map.
[01:05] Lina: thanks, quick clarifying q: are you currently using any managed LLM API or self-hosting?
[01:10] Maya: currently mixed. we use a hosted api for non-sensitive traffic but self-host core flows. we want to reduce ops burden while keeping strong guarantees. encryption and audit logs are critical for compliance.
[01:22] Ethan: understood, and team size/ on call?
[01:25] Samir: small oncall, so automation is key. we can't babysit replicas across regions manually.

[02:00] Lina: ok, let me walk through patterns we typically recommend. one: hosted primary with dedicated fallback — route most traffic to hosted for cost and scale, but pipeline critical routes to dedicated pools or private nodes with guaranteed capacity; two: multi-region active/active routing with automatic failover by region; three: model-variant fallbacks — if a heavy model times out, we fall back to a smaller quantized variant. we also put circuit-breaker policies and retries with exponential backoff.
[02:45] Maya: can you be more concrete about routing? like DNS? load balancer? how fast is failover?
[02:52] Lina: we do policy-based routing at the control plane. you can define route policies by latency, region, customer tier. on health events we can failover in tens of seconds for control-plane detected failures. for network partitions we do region-based routing — traffic routed to the next healthy region. if a model endpoint degrades we route to a compatible model variant automatically.
[03:18] Samir: tens of seconds is ok, but what about in-flight requests? will they get killed or retried? we need idempotency guarantees because some requests hit downstream billing systems.
[03:30] Ethan: good point. we expose per-route timeouts and retry policies. for critical ops we recommend synchronous timeouts + client-side retry idempotency tokens. on a failover the control plane will return a 503 or retry three times depending on policy, and we support request-level replay where it's safe.
[04:05] Jordan: and SLOs — what SLA do you offer for hosted vs dedicated?
[04:10] Lina: hosted has standard uptime commitments and we publish performance profiles. Dedicated comes with a contractual SLA — typically 99.9% for uptime depending on commit, with options for higher. Private on-prem is supported but SLA depends on the customer's infra and we provide operational runbooks and support packages.
[04:30] Maya: 99.9% is a starting point yes; we need RTO targets for region failover — like recover within 1 minute for user-visible failures, or at least degrade gracefully.
[04:42] Lina: for user-visible failover to another region 1 minute is aggressive; realistically control-plane detection plus routing usually takes 30-90s depending on propagation and warm caches. we recommend proactive cross-region warm pools: keep a small warm dedicated capacity in secondary region so failover doesn't cold-start model weights. that meets near-1-minute goals for many workloads.
[05:12] Samir: warm pools — what's the cost tradeoff and how do you size them?
[05:18] Ethan: sizing is workload dependent; our Optimize tooling gives suggestions based on qps and seq length distribution. warm pools cost is basically reserved capacity pricing; typical pattern is 5-15% of primary capacity as warm standby.

[06:00] Maya: auditability & logs: we need full audit trails for inference requests tied to customer IDs, and encryption at rest with KMS. also SSO for control plane.
[06:12] Lina: yes — private deployments include KMS/HSM integrations and we support SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning. hosted supports envelope encryption with customer-managed keys for enterprise tiers. audit logs for inference events and control plane actions are available and can be exported to your SIEM.
[06:35] Jordan: do audit logs include payloads? we have privacy constraints.
[06:40] Lina: payload capture is configurable — by default we log metadata (request id, model, latency, status). full payload logging requires explicit enablement and can be routed to customer-controlled storage in Private.

[07:15] Samir: let's talk about model fallbacks — we need consistent answers or at least trustable degradation. if we fall back to a smaller quantized model responses can materially differ. how do you monitor quality regressions?
[07:30] Lina: we pair fallback rules with evaluation hooks. Redwood Optimize can run canary evals on a sample prompt set and emit quality deltas; you can set thresholds to prevent automatic fallback if quality drop exceeds a threshold. also canary traffic routing (percentage split) helps validate fallbacks before full switch.
[08:02] Maya: and what about rate limiting and throttling across regions?
[08:06] Ethan: rate limiting is per-account and per-route. with multi-region deployments we have consistent global quotas and local burst windows; we can also set per-region caps.

[09:00] Jordan: do you support circuit breakers so we don't overload downstream systems when the model slowness cascades?
[09:06] Lina: yes — circuit breakers at route level, with configurable thresholds and automatic fallback to cached responses or a simpler model. you can also configure a degraded response template so UX is controlled.
[09:30] Samir: caching — we have a lot of repeated prefixes so KV/prefix cache would cut token cost and latency. how is cache invalidation managed across regions?
[09:40] Lina: we have prefix/KV cache with TTLs. for multi-region caches we support eventual consistency by default; for strong consistency you can configure a primary-region write with replication, but that increases latency. most customers use eventual consistency with short TTLs for inference.

[11:00] Maya: one more ops question — how do you run incident simulations? we'd like to run a scheduled failover test without impacting customers.
[11:12] Ethan: we recommend a staged POC: 1) synthetic load tests simulating region outage, 2) control-plane failover drills with canary traffic, 3) measure p50/p95/p99 and error rates. we can run this with a sandbox account. we'll also provide a runbook so your oncall can practice the sequence.
[11:40] Samir: do you support traffic shadowing? we'd like to validate model behavior in private environment.
[11:46] Lina: yes, traffic shadowing to a private deployment is supported; it costs for traffic processed but it's invaluable for regression testing.

[13:00] Jordan: procurement question — if we choose Dedicated with reserved pools, what are contract/commit expectations?
[13:12] Ethan: dedicated typically requires a monthly or annual commit for capacity; we have burst options for headroom. pricing will vary by GPU class and region. for initial POC we often do a short trial with commit offsets to lower friction.

[14:00] Maya: i'd like to understand a concrete failure scenario: primary region network partition while model endpoints are healthy but control plane partial loss. how would requests be handled?
[14:15] Lina: if control-plane can't reach the primary region, regional routing will attempt a secondary region with warm standby. requests already in flight may time out; our client SDK supports retry with idempotency tokens. for control-plane loss we have a read-only fallback where edge proxies route based on last-known policy for a short window. for longer control-plane outages we'd route to a preconfigured secondary management endpoint.
[14:50] Samir: and how do you detect model degradation vs infra issues?
[14:55] Lina: we collect model-level metrics (latency, token generation rate, error codes) and infra metrics (GPU utilization, host errors). anomaly detection flags patterns — e.g., model timeouts across healthy hosts means model load or memory pressure; host errors across models suggests infra. our dashboard surfaces correlated signals.

[16:00] Ethan: operationally, for critical routes we recommend: 1) model variant fallback with quality gating, 2) warm standby region capacity, 3) per-route circuit breakers, and 4) synthetic canary tests and runbooks.

[18:00] Maya: what about data residency? some EU customers require data stay in EU. can you guarantee region pinning?
[18:06] Lina: yes — routing policies can pin traffic to regions, and Private deployments give full control. hosted enterprise tenants can opt into region-restricted deployments with contractual assurances.

[19:30] Jordan: are there observability hooks we can plug into our existing tracing?
[19:36] Lina: yes — we emit traces and support OpenTelemetry headers. you can correlate request traces end-to-end. logs and metrics can be exported to your Prometheus/Grafana and logs to your SIEM.

[21:00] Samir: any gotchas with VPC/private connectivity? VPNs, peering, latency?
[21:08] Ethan: Private has a customer-managed network. typical setup is a VPC peering or private link to our private control plane. network latency depends on your datacenter to our region; for ultra-low-latency you can do on-prem package. we provide recommended network MTU and keepalive settings in the runbook.

[23:00] Maya: ok let's talk next steps — we'd like a POC that validates failover and fallback behavior with a sample of our prompts and data governance requirements.
[23:12] Ethan: perfect — proposed plan: 1) share sample prompt set and traffic profile, 2) we'll provision a sandbox with hosted primary + dedicated warm standby in a second region, 3) run synthetic failover tests and traffic shadowing, 4) run canary evals for fallback quality.

[23:40] Jordan: timeline — we want results before end of quarter, so 6 weeks ideally.
[23:48] Ethan: that's doable. we'll aim to start provisioning next week.

[24:30] Lina: i'll also share security docs (SOC 2, encryption, KMS integration guide) and the runbook for failover tests.

[25:10] Samir: also please include config samples for circuit breakers, retry policies, and example rollout for model fallback thresholds.
[25:22] Ethan: will do.

[26:00] Maya: any specific questions from your side for us?
[26:05] Lina: just one: what are the top 3 routes by volume and their acceptable p99 targets?
[26:12] Jordan: 1) support chat (p99 < 700ms), 2) ticket triage (p99 < 1.2s), 3) agent assist (p99 < 500ms for snippets).

[27:00] Ethan: thank you, we have enough to draft the POC scope and pricing sketch. we'll also include failure injection test plan.

[28:00] Maya: and include who from our side will be responsible — i'll be overall owner, samir will own oncall/runbooks, jordan product will track success criteria.

[29:00] Ethan: great, i'll recap next steps now.
[29:05] Ethan: recap: share sample prompts/traffic, redwood to provision sandbox with hosted primary + dedicated warm standby in secondary region, run synthetic failover + traffic shadowing, run canary evals for fallback quality, share security docs and circuit breaker configs. aim to start provisioning next week, target 6-week results.

[30:00] Jordan: sounds good.
[30:10] Maya: also please include expected cost estimate for warm standby sizing and data egress.
[30:18] Ethan: we'll include a cost appendix.
[31:00] Lina: i'll follow up with links to security pack and a sample runbook.

[32:00] Samir: one last nit: in the runbook can you include clear rollback steps if fallback causes bad outputs?
[32:08] Lina: yes, rollback is part of rollout policy — automatic rollback on quality regression and manual steps documented.

[33:00] Ethan: any other items?
[33:05] Maya: no, thanks. this was helpful.
[33:10] Ethan: great, we'll send the POC statement of work and schedule next sync. thanks everyone.

[33:30] (meeting ends)
